text: Construct the argument first — who is arriving, what they already believe, what they must come to believe, what single action closes the decision, and what evidence carries each step. Then build ONLY the sections that argument needs, and delete everything else.
Use the actual offer, traffic and available evidence to choose the number of links, sections and form fields. These are design decisions, not guaranteed conversion lifts or universal numerical rules.
establish five things: Traffic source … Audience … Offer … Action … Evidence
note: Site plan block has Reader, Insight, Priorities, Offer and action, Proof, Sections, Left out (D1); no traffic source.

text: make reversible design assumptions and record them … Do not invent an offer, destination, target identity or evidence. If the requested action has no supported destination, continue a useful draft and report that conversion gap. Ask only for a missing decision that changes the argument and cannot be resolved from available context.

Where the page must START depends on what the visitor already knows. The classic ladder (Eugene Schwartz's stages of awareness) is the tool: Unaware … Problem-aware … Solution-aware … Product-aware … Most-aware

Traffic source is your best clue to stage: a narrow paid-search click is usually solution- or product-aware; a cold outbound recipient is usually problem-aware at best; a retargeted visitor has seen the offer before.

Choose the amount of chrome from the page's task; a separate navigation bar is not required. … The native shell … The minimal campaign shell … A hero-led campaign can integrate the seller identity into its opening composition and omit a separate navigation bar
Target identity belongs in the opening content outside navigation: a restrained eyebrow, account bar or lockup above the main heading. … A target logo is not a navigation item.
note: Opposite of site D3 "Never put the account's logo anywhere else on the page" and D2 "Prepared for" in the header.

text: If any answer is no — mixed traffic, a general marketing page, a page meant for exploration — the native shell almost always stays. … Does the navigation help THIS visitor verify trust — or does it only give them ways to abandon the argument?

Account-personalized (ABM) pages get no automatic answer. … Decide per page, from acquisition context and the trust question; say which you chose and why in your report; and if the user told you which shell they want, that is the answer.
Shell choice is independent of page LENGTH. A minimal shell can carry a long, decision-complete argument … The shell removes exits; it never removes information the decision needs.

A pattern is a theory of why this visitor converts. Pick by acquisition context and available evidence — never by preference. … Search-intent mirror … Conversion scent … Radical simplification … Complex made simple … Proof stack … Deadline urgency … Video-led … Visual product-led … Incentive capture
**Video-led** | Motion explains it faster than words | Headline still states the promise; page works without pressing play
note: Site D1 lists "brand videos" among sections to remove.

text: the page never invents evidence. No fabricated customers, metrics, quotes, awards, deadlines, or partnership implications … When a section you want needs proof that does not exist, cut the section or reshape it around what is real.

Each section must answer exactly one visitor question: What is this? → hero · Why me, why now? → relevance / priorities · How does it work? → explanation / architecture · Why should I believe it? → proof beside the claim · What do I do? → the offer and the action
note: Same five as the site's default shape (D1 5.1–5.5).

text: Order the survivors by the awareness stage: the visitor's next unanswered question is always the next section.

Page length follows decision complexity: a considered enterprise purchase may justify seven sections; a high-intent giveaway justifies three. Never pad a page to feel complete, and never cut information the decision genuinely needs.
note: Site D1: "usual shape is five sections … rarely more than 600 words"; "Sections: up to five".

text: research must change the visible explanation of relevance, mechanism, proof or evaluation. A minimal shell is not a reason to produce a thin page.

When a whole-page campaign adaptation authorizes structural changes, a section answering NO question in the argument may be **removed**. On a scoped edit, preserve sections outside the request and report broader suggestions instead.
**One primary conversion action.** Repeat its chosen label and supported action/destination consistently. … Navigation, legal and relevant trust/resource links can serve their separate jobs.
**Place actions at natural decision points** — after the promise, after the explanation, at the close — not after every band.
**Forms ask only what the next step needs.** … Do not promise consent, storage, delivery timing or follow-up behavior the implementation does not establish.

Account-specific pages need the appropriate publication posture. Preserve supported account markers and the existing noindex policy on derived ABM pages. … Public segment/event pages follow their brief.

read the finished page top to bottom AS THE ARRIVING VISITOR. At every scroll position ask: do I know what this is? do I know why it's for me? has every claim shown me its evidence? do I know exactly what I get if I act?
Report what you chose and why, briefly: the pattern, the shell posture, the assumed brief elements, the sections cut and added, and any evidence you declined to fabricate.
